claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Moderate cooling of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 produces nanoscale solute clusters within the BCC matrix because atomic mobility is limited.
The nanoscale solute clusters act as preferential nucleation sites for secondary phases during subsequent thermal exposure.
Cooling rates that permit moderate diffusion but not full thermodynamic phase separation favor nanoscale solute clustering.
Extremely rapid quenching leaves the BCC state largely chemically homogeneous.
Local solute segregation during moderate cooling forms pre-precipitation regions.
Pre-existing solute clusters lower the nucleation-energy barrier for secondary phases.
During isothermal aging, the clusters enable heterogeneous nucleation of secondary phases.
Slow-cooled and aged samples will contain significantly more nanoscale solute clusters than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled and aged samples will exhibit significantly more secondary-phase formation than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will largely retain a uniform BCC phase with minimal clustering or secondary-phase formation.
The proposed clustering-mediated mechanism may cease to describe the transformation under prolonged exposures that lead to equilibrium.
TEM, XRD, and atom-probe tomography can distinguish the predicted microstructural and chemical differences between the cooling treatments.
Failure of the slowly cooled and aged samples to show a statistically significant increase in either clusters or secondary phases relative to the quenched samples would falsify the hypothesis.
